subject: biology
topicDisplay: Core Concepts Assessed Across All Components
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which factor would DECREASE the rate of transpiration from a leaf?
questions.explain: Higher humidity reduces the water-potential gradient between the leaf air spaces and the atmosphere, slowing diffusion of water vapour out.

questions.q: On a graph of reaction rate against temperature for a human enzyme, the rate rises to a peak around 37 C then falls sharply. The sharp fall above 40 C is best explained by:
options: denaturation as bonds maintaining the active site break
a continued increase in kinetic energy
questions.explain: Beyond the optimum, excessive vibration breaks the hydrogen and ionic bonds holding the tertiary structure, denaturing the active site and sharply reducing activity.

questions.q: The site of translation in a eukaryotic cell is the:
questions.explain: Translation occurs at ribosomes, where mRNA codons are read to assemble a polypeptide.

questions.q: In phloem, the mass-flow hypothesis explains translocation as a result of:
options: Active loading of sucrose at the source lowering water potential, drawing in water and raising hydrostatic pressure that drives flow to the sink
Diffusion of sucrose from source to sink
Capillary action in the sieve tubes
questions.explain: Sucrose loaded at the source lowers water potential so water enters by osmosis, raising pressure and forcing sap toward sinks where sucrose is unloaded.

questions.q: A phospholipid differs from a triglyceride in that a phospholipid has:
options: only ester bonds and no hydrophilic region
three fatty acids attached to glycerol
one fatty acid replaced by a phosphate-containing hydrophilic group
questions.explain: In a phospholipid, one of the three fatty acids of a triglyceride is replaced by a hydrophilic phosphate group, making the molecule amphipathic.

questions.q: The very large surface area of the small intestine for absorption is produced by:
options: Villi and microvilli on the epithelial cells
A dense capillary network in the submucosa only
questions.explain: Folded villi each covered in microvilli (the brush border) massively increase the absorptive surface area of the ileum.

questions.q: What is the role of DNA helicase during replication?
options: Proofreading newly added bases for errors
Adding free nucleotides in a 3' to 5' direction
Breaking the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases to unwind the double helix
Joining adjacent nucleotides with phosphodiester bonds
questions.explain: Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, separating the two strands of the double helix.

questions.q: During ventricular systole, the atrioventricular valves close because:
options: The ventricles are relaxing and filling
questions.explain: As the ventricles contract their pressure rises above that of the atria, forcing the AV valves shut to prevent backflow.

questions.q: Below the optimum temperature, the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction is low mainly because:
options: substrate and enzyme molecules have less kinetic energy, so successful collisions forming complexes are less frequent
the active site has changed shape permanently
questions.explain: At lower temperatures molecules move more slowly, reducing the frequency of effective collisions and the formation of enzyme-substrate complexes.

questions.q: A prosthetic group differs from a coenzyme in that a prosthetic group is:
options: a permanently and tightly bound non-protein component of the enzyme
always an inorganic metal ion in solution
questions.explain: A prosthetic group is permanently bound to the enzyme (e.g. FAD in some dehydrogenases), unlike a coenzyme which associates only transiently.

questions.q: During translation, the bond formed between adjacent amino acids on the ribosome is a:
questions.explain: Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds in a condensation reaction catalysed at the ribosome.

questions.q: How many hydrogen bonds form between guanine and cytosine in DNA?
questions.explain: Guanine and cytosine pair via three hydrogen bonds, whereas adenine and thymine pair via two.

questions.q: ATP is described as the universal energy currency because:
options: it stores energy long-term like glycogen
its hydrolysis releases a large, fixed amount of energy in a single immediate step
hydrolysis of its terminal phosphate releases a manageable quantity of energy for cellular reactions
it cannot be regenerated once hydrolysed
questions.explain: ATP releases a small, usable amount of energy when its terminal phosphate bond is hydrolysed to ADP and Pi, and is rapidly resynthesised.

questions.q: Glycogen and amylose both store glucose, but glycogen is more highly branched. A direct consequence of this branching is that glycogen:
options: can be hydrolysed more rapidly because of more terminal glucose residues
forms straight chains that pack into fibres
questions.explain: More branch points give more free ends from which glucose can be released quickly, suiting the high metabolic rate of animals.

questions.q: Two enzymes catalyse the same reaction; enzyme X has a lower Km and a lower Vmax than enzyme Y. This means enzyme X:
options: binds substrate more readily but has a lower maximum rate when saturated
binds substrate less readily but works faster when saturated
questions.explain: A lower Km means higher affinity (binds substrate at low concentration), while a lower Vmax means a slower maximum rate once saturated.

questions.q: In PCR, the temperature is raised to around 95 degrees C in order to:
options: Separate the two DNA strands by breaking hydrogen bonds
questions.explain: Denaturation at ~95 degrees C breaks the hydrogen bonds, separating the DNA into single strands.

questions.q: The secondary structure of a protein (alpha-helix and beta-pleated sheet) is stabilised primarily by:
options: hydrogen bonds between the C=O and N-H groups of the backbone
questions.explain: Secondary structure arises from regular hydrogen bonding between backbone carbonyl and amine groups, independent of R-group identity.

questions.q: The biuret test detects proteins by producing a purple colour, which results from:
options: the formation of a complex between copper(II) ions and peptide bonds in alkaline conditions
the breakdown of peptide bonds by acid
copper ions reducing to copper oxide
questions.explain: In alkaline solution, copper(II) ions form a violet coordination complex with the nitrogen atoms of peptide bonds.

questions.q: Fetal haemoglobin has a dissociation curve to the LEFT of adult haemoglobin because:
options: It must release oxygen more readily to the placenta
It is less saturated at every partial pressure of oxygen
It has a higher affinity for oxygen, allowing it to load oxygen from maternal blood at the placenta
questions.explain: A higher oxygen affinity (curve to the left) lets fetal Hb take up oxygen from maternal Hb across the placenta.

questions.q: Many enzymes require a cofactor such as a metal ion (e.g. Zn2+ or Cl-) because the cofactor:
options: denatures the enzyme to expose the active site
is a non-protein component needed for the enzyme to function
questions.explain: Cofactors are non-protein helpers required for catalytic activity, sometimes altering the active site shape to allow binding.

questions.q: Most tissue fluid is returned to the circulation by the:
options: Active transport across the capillary wall
Venule end of the capillary only, driven by osmosis
Combination of osmotic return at the venule end and drainage by the lymphatic system
questions.explain: Some fluid re-enters at the venule end down a water-potential gradient, and the excess is collected and returned by the lymphatic system.

questions.q: What is the function of the non-conducting (fibrous) tissue between the atria and ventricles?
options: To delay and channel the impulse through the AVN so the ventricles contract after the atria
To speed conduction directly from atria to ventricles
To prevent blood entering the ventricles
To act as a second pacemaker
questions.explain: The fibrous ring stops the impulse passing directly to the ventricles, forcing it through the AVN, ensuring atria empty before ventricles contract.

questions.q: Increased methylation of DNA in a gene's promoter region typically results in:
options: A change in the DNA base sequence
questions.explain: Promoter methylation usually prevents transcription factor binding, inhibiting transcription without altering the base sequence.

questions.q: Which type of bond is NOT involved in stabilising the tertiary structure of a globular protein?
questions.explain: Tertiary structure is held by hydrogen, ionic and disulfide bonds plus hydrophobic interactions; phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides, not amino acids.

questions.q: When investigating the effect of substrate concentration on enzyme rate, why is it important to use a buffer solution?
options: to keep pH constant so that pH does not act as an uncontrolled variable affecting the active site
to act as a competitive inhibitor
questions.explain: A buffer maintains constant pH, controlling a variable that would otherwise alter the enzyme's tertiary structure and confound results.

questions.q: Hydrogen bonding between water molecules arises because water is:
options: a polar molecule with a partially negative oxygen and partially positive hydrogens
an ionic compound that dissociates fully
a non-polar molecule with even charge distribution
questions.explain: Unequal sharing of electrons makes oxygen slightly negative and hydrogens slightly positive, allowing hydrogen bonds between adjacent water molecules.

questions.q: At high substrate concentration with fixed enzyme concentration, the rate of reaction plateaus because:
options: all active sites are occupied so enzyme concentration becomes the limiting factor
questions.explain: When substrate is in excess, every active site is continually occupied, so the number of enzyme molecules limits the rate.

questions.q: In the formation of a phosphodiester bond between two nucleotides, the bond forms between:
options: the base of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next
the phosphate group of one nucleotide and the deoxyribose of the adjacent nucleotide
questions.explain: A condensation reaction links the phosphate of one nucleotide to the sugar of the next, forming the sugar-phosphate backbone.

questions.q: In contrast, increasing the concentration of a NON-COMPETITIVE inhibitor would:
options: increase the enzyme's affinity for substrate
reduce Vmax because raising substrate cannot displace the inhibitor
questions.explain: Because non-competitive inhibitors do not compete for the active site, additional substrate cannot reverse their effect, so Vmax is reduced.

questions.q: On a Michaelis-Menten curve, the Km value of an enzyme represents the substrate concentration at which:
options: the reaction rate is half of Vmax
questions.explain: Km is the substrate concentration giving half the maximum rate; a low Km indicates a high affinity of the enzyme for its substrate.
